directAnswer: St. Innocent I was pope from 401 to 417, through the Visigothic sack of Rome in 410. He defended the exiled St. John Chrysostom, condemned the teachings of Pelagius at the request of the African bishops, and wrote influential letters on the canon of Scripture, confirmation, and the anointing of the sick. He was born at Albano near Rome, and his feast is kept on March 12.

paras: Innocent's reign coincided with the collapse of Roman security in Italy. Alaric's Visigoths besieged Rome more than once, and the emperor Honorius stayed safely at Ravenna. During one round of negotiations, Innocent traveled to Ravenna as part of an embassy from the city seeking terms.

He was still away when Alaric's forces entered and sacked Rome in August 410, the first time the city had fallen to a foreign enemy in some eight centuries. The shock reverberated across the Christian world and later moved St. Augustine to write The City of God. Innocent returned to help the city recover.

In the East, John Chrysostom, archbishop of Constantinople, was deposed in 403 and later exiled through the efforts of Theophilus of Alexandria and the imperial court. John appealed to Innocent, who refused to recognize the deposition and demanded a fair hearing by a council of Eastern and Western bishops.

Innocent sent a delegation to Constantinople, but its members were mistreated and sent back. He broke communion with the bishops responsible. John died in exile in 407, and Innocent restored communion only after his name was restored to the church's commemorations.

The British monk Pelagius taught that human beings could live without sin by their own effort, minimizing the need for grace. In 416, councils at Carthage and Milevis in North Africa, with Augustine among the bishops, condemned his views and asked Innocent to confirm their judgment.

In early 417, Innocent replied that Pelagius and his disciple Caelestius were to be excluded from communion until they repented, and praised the Africans for referring the matter to the Apostolic See. Augustine later spoke of the case as settled once Rome's reply arrived, a remark frequently remembered in simplified form.

In 405 Innocent answered Bishop Exuperius of Toulouse with a list of the books of Scripture that matches the canon later affirmed by the Church. In 416 he wrote to Bishop Decentius of Gubbio about liturgical practice, teaching that the anointing with chrism on the forehead after baptism belongs to bishops and citing the Letter of James on the anointing of the sick.
He also supported the bishop of Thessalonica as his representative in eastern Illyricum. Innocent died on March 12, 417, and was buried in the Catacomb of Pontian.

keyFacts: Pope from 401 to 417; born at Albano near Rome
Rome was sacked by Alaric's Visigoths in 410 while he was at Ravenna
Defended St. John Chrysostom and broke communion with his persecutors
Confirmed the African condemnation of Pelagius and Caelestius in 417
Wrote on the canon of Scripture (405) and on confirmation and anointing (416)

faqs.question: Where was Pope Innocent I during the sack of Rome?
faqs.answer: He was in Ravenna, where he had gone as part of an embassy to Emperor Honorius seeking a settlement with Alaric. The city fell in August 410 while he was away.

faqs.question: What did Pope Innocent I decide about Pelagius?
faqs.answer: In 417 he confirmed the judgment of African councils that Pelagius and Caelestius had taught error regarding grace, and declared them out of communion until they repented.

faqs.question: What is Innocent I's letter to Decentius about?
faqs.answer: Written in 416 to the bishop of Gubbio, it explains Roman liturgical customs, including the bishop's role in anointing the baptized with chrism and the anointing of the sick based on the Letter of James.
